To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the consistency of Facebook's replicated storage system is stronger than previously reported; (2) the performance of the system is significantly affected by consistency; and (3) the consistency of the system can be measured and improved.

(1) Facebook’s consistency model is weaker than most people think; (2) Facebook’s consistency is strong enough to prevent most user-visible anomalies; (3) Facebook users experience many more user-visible anomalies due to bugs in the client and the server, than due to the consistency model; (4) the consistency of Facebook is strong enough to support a large class of applications, including many that have traditionally been thought to require strong consistency.

the consistency of the Facebook social graph is strong enough to be invisible to most users, and that it is possible to quantify this strength in a way that is meaningful for both the users and the developers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
measuring and understanding consistency in large Web services.
the following question: How much stronger consistency do we need in order to prevent anomalies?
measuring and understanding the consistency of Facebook’s replicated storage system, and with understanding its impact on Facebook’s users and developers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stronger consistency reduces the frequency and severity of anomalies.
, for the applications we have studied, the performance cost of strong consistency was negligible.
, in practice, stronger consistency does not come at a large performance cost.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, at the scale of Facebook, stronger forms of consistency are not worth the price of weaker performance properties, and weaker consistency is not worth the cost of higher complexity and higher likelihood of anomalies.
we have developed and deployed an approach to quantify consistency and its trade-off against performance.

, for the Facebook Web service, stronger consistency does not significantly increase the number of anomalies, but it does significantly increase programming complexity, and thus, we recommend using the strongest form of consistency that does not increase anomalies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stronger consistency has a significant cost, and that this cost can vary widely depending on the consistency property.
stronger consistency does not come for free, even at Facebook's scale.
, at least in the Facebook setting, stronger consistency does not significantly increase programming complexity.
